meta.title: Who really said "One person can make a difference, and every person should try"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Widely pinned on JFK, but the JFK Library traces the words to Jacqueline Kennedy, who wrote them about her husband — Look magazine credited her in 1966.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'One person can make a difference, and every person should try'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a JFK line. His widow Jacqueline wrote it about his beliefs; Look credited her in 1966. RFK popularized it in 1968. The JFK Library found no evidence JFK said it.

answer.label: Not John F. Kennedy — written by Jacqueline Kennedy
answer.authorDates: 1929–1994 · U.S. First Lady, describing her late husband’s beliefs
answer.sourceLine: The exact wording traces not to the President but to his widow. For a Kennedy Library exhibit in the mid-1960s, Jacqueline Kennedy wrote that “he believed that one man can make a difference — and that every man should try,” and Look magazine correctly credited her in 1966. The JFK Library’s own archivists found no concrete evidence that JFK himself ever said or wrote it; the gender-neutral ‘person’ wording is a later rephrasing that drifted onto his name by the 1980s.

source.excerpt: He believed that one man can make a difference — and that every man should try.
trail: The JFK Library Archives investigated the line and found no concrete evidence John F. Kennedy ever said or wrote it.
Per the same JFK Library account, Jacqueline Kennedy authored the statement for a Library exhibit and Look magazine correctly credited her in 1966.
Reference works echo this: Respectfully Quoted (1989) lists “One man can make a difference and every man should try” under Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis.
source.excerptNote: Jacqueline Kennedy’s original wording, describing her husband’s beliefs. The familiar ‘one person…every person should try’ is a later, gender-neutral rewording pinned onto JFK himself.

source.rightsNote: The documented wording was written by Jacqueline Kennedy and first published in Look magazine in 1966 — well after 1931 — so the specific phrasing is in copyright, not public domain. The later gender-neutral ‘one person…every person’ variant is an unattributed paraphrase with no identified source.

author.name: Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis
author.heading: The First Lady behind the line
author.bio: Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis was First Lady of the United States from 1961 to 1963 and, after the assassinations of her husband and brother-in-law, a longtime book editor in New York. In the mid-1960s she wrote a statement for a traveling Kennedy Library exhibit summarizing her late husband’s convictions — the passage from which this widely misattributed ‘one person can make a difference’ quote descends.

misattribution.heading: How a wife’s tribute became her husband’s quote
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most durable Kennedy misquotes — and unusually, its true origin is fully documented by the Kennedy family’s own library.

items.why: The line appears in none of JFK’s documented speeches or writings and is almost always quoted undated. The JFK Library Archives report finding no concrete evidence he ever said it; writers only began stating “JFK said” the line directly around the early 1980s.

During his 1968 presidential campaign, RFK told Idaho State University students that “one man can make a difference and that every man should try,” and used the line so often that it became closely tied to him as well, per the JFK Library Archives.

misattribution.truthLine: The words were written by Jacqueline Kennedy to describe her husband’s outlook, and were correctly credited to her when Look printed them in 1966; reference works such as Respectfully Quoted still list the line under her name.

context.heading: Why this one is worth getting right
lead: The sentiment is so on-brand for John F. Kennedy’s call to public service that few readers question it — which is exactly how a tribute written about him became a quote by him. The actual author, Jacqueline Kennedy, was characterizing a belief she attributed to her husband, not reporting a sentence he spoke.
The Kennedy Library itself flags the line as unverified for JFK, an unusually clean case where the misattribution can be traced sentence by sentence back to its real source.
context.detailsSummary: The wording’s drift, step by step
detailsBody: Mid-1960s: Jacqueline Kennedy writes the statement for a traveling Kennedy Library exhibit: “He believed that one man can make a difference — and that every man should try.”
1966: Look magazine prints it, correctly crediting Jacqueline Kennedy.
1968: Robert F. Kennedy adopts a near-identical line on the campaign trail, cementing the family association.
Early 1980s onward: Newspapers and, later, mugs and posters begin attributing the line directly to John F. Kennedy, often in the gender-neutral ‘one person…every person’ form.
